content: The body louse, scientifically known as Pediculus humanus humanus (or sometimes referred to as Pediculus humanus corporis), is a parasitic insect that infests humans. The condition of being infested with lice—whether head lice, body lice, or pubic lice—is termed pediculosis. The genome of the body louse was sequenced and published in 2010. Morphologically, Pediculus humanus humanus (the body louse) is indistinguishable from Pediculus humanus capitis (the head louse). However, these two types of lice will only interbreed under laboratory conditions. In their natural environments, they occupy distinct habitats. Body lice have adapted to attach their eggs to clothing, whereas head lice attach their eggs to the base of human hairs. The life cycle of the body louse consists of three stages: egg (also called a nit), nymph, and adult. Nits are the eggs of lice. They are typically visible in the seams of an infested person’s clothing, especially around the waistline, under the armpits, or even in body hair. Nits are oval in shape and range in color from yellow to white. Body lice nits generally take 1 to 2 weeks to hatch. Nymphs are immature lice that emerge from the nits. A nymph resembles an adult body louse but is smaller in size. Nymphs mature into adults approximately 9 to 12 days after hatching. To survive, nymphs must feed on blood. Adult body lice are about the size of a sesame seed (2.5–3.5 mm in length), have six legs, and are tan to grayish-white in color. Female lice lay eggs. Like nymphs, adult lice must feed on blood to survive. If separated from their human hosts, lice cannot survive at room temperature and will die. The body louse is believed to have diverged from the head louse approximately 100,000 years ago, which coincides with the estimated time of the origin of clothing in human history. Body lice were first formally described by Carl Linnaeus in the 10th edition of Systema Naturae.
